title: Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette take the throne
text:
On 10 May 1774, the old king Louis XV dies. His grandson becomes King of France under the name Louis XVI. He is only 19 years old! He is said to have cried out: "Dear God, protect us, we are too young to reign!"

Louis XVI is shy, kind and serious. He loves hunting, geography and, above all, making locks: he spends hours in his workshop making locks and keys! But he finds it hard to make decisions.

His wife, Marie Antoinette, is an Austrian princess, the daughter of Empress Maria Theresa. She was married at 14 to bring France and Austria closer together, after they had long been enemies. She is pretty and cheerful, and she loves fashion, music and parties. She has a little fairy-tale village built for herself in the park of Versailles: the Queen's Hamlet.

The king is an [absolute monarch]: he has all the power. He makes the laws, decides on war and peace, and can even have someone thrown in prison without a trial, using a "lettre de cachet" (a sealed letter). People say he is king "by divine right", which means chosen by God.

The royal court lives in the Palace of Versailles, in luxury, far from the people of Paris and the countryside.

At first, the French love their young king and hope he will make their lives better. But the kingdom has big problems: it is short of money, taxes are unfair, and new ideas about freedom are spreading.

Nobody knows yet that this king will be the last king of the Old Regime, and that everything is about to change in just a few years...

title: Clergy, nobles and Third Estate: an unequal society
text:
Before the Revolution, French society is divided into three groups called the three "estates" (or "orders"). You are born into an estate, and it is almost impossible to change.

The First Estate is the [clergy]: bishops, priests, monks and nuns. They pray and look after churches, schools and hospitals. The Church is very rich: it owns lots of land and collects the tithe, a tax paid by peasants.

The Second Estate is the [nobility]: the nobles, the lords. There are about 400,000 of them. Long ago, they fought for the king. Many live on their lands, others at the court of Versailles.

These two estates have [privileges]: they pay almost no taxes, they have reserved jobs in the army or the Church, and nobles receive dues paid by the peasants.

The Third Estate is... everybody else! Peasants, craftsmen, workers, shopkeepers, but also rich bankers, doctors and lawyers, who are called the [bourgeoisie]. Together they make up 98% of the French people. We call this whole group the [Third Estate].

It is the Third Estate that pays almost all the taxes: the taille for the king, the tithe for the Church, and feudal dues for the nobles. There is even the gabelle, a tax on salt, which people need to preserve meat!

The peasants, who are the largest group, often live in poverty. When the harvest is bad, they go hungry.

A famous cartoon from the time shows an old, bent peasant carrying a priest and a noble on his back. It says: "Let's hope this game will soon be over."

Many members of the bourgeoisie, rich and educated, find it unfair that they do not have the same rights as the nobles.

title: The ideas of the Enlightenment
text:
In the 18th century, thinkers known as the [Enlightenment philosophers] have new ideas. They want to light up people's minds with [reason], like a light chasing away the darkness.

Voltaire makes fun of injustice and intolerance. He writes: "Crush the infamous thing!", meaning fanaticism. He defends people who have been unfairly convicted.

Montesquieu explains that all power should not be given to one single person. The one who makes the laws, the one who carries them out and the one who judges should be different people: this is the [separation of powers].

In 1762, Jean-Jacques Rousseau writes The Social Contract. It begins: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." For him, power must come from the people, from the "general will", and not from a king.

Diderot and d'Alembert publish the Encyclopédie, which gathers all the knowledge of the time and criticises privileges.

These ideas spread everywhere: in books, newspapers, salons where people hold discussions, cafés and clubs. Even when some books are banned, people read them in secret.

Little by little, more and more French people start asking questions: why should the king have all the power? Why should nobles have more rights than others? Why can't people choose their own religion?

Not all the philosophers wanted a revolution. In fact, Voltaire and Rousseau both died in 1778, eleven years before 1789. But their ideas of liberty, equality and tolerance will inspire the revolutionaries.

People often say that the Enlightenment "prepared minds" for the Revolution.

title: France helps the Americans become free
refs: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
text:
On the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, thirteen British colonies in America rebel against the King of England. On 4 July 1776, they declare their independence: the United States of America is born!

Their [Declaration of Independence] says that "all men are created equal" and that they have a right to "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness". These are the ideas of the Enlightenment put into practice!

A young French nobleman, the Marquis de Lafayette, is thrilled. At 19, he buys a ship with his own money and sails off to fight alongside George Washington. He becomes a hero in America.

In 1778, King Louis XVI decides to help the Americans officially. Above all, he wants revenge on England, which had defeated France a few years earlier. France sends soldiers, ships and a great deal of money.

In 1781, at Yorktown, the American and French armies, with the fleet of Admiral de Grasse, win a great victory. In 1783, England recognises the independence of the United States.

This war has two important consequences for France.

First, it was very expensive: about a billion livres! The royal treasury is empty.

Second, the French soldiers and officers coming back from America have seen that a people can free itself from a king and give itself a [constitution]. They bring these ideas back to France.

Lafayette will play a big role at the start of the Revolution. He is called "the hero of the two worlds".

title: The treasury is empty
text:
In the 1780s, the kingdom of France has a huge problem: it has run out of money! It spends much more than it earns. This is called a [deficit].

Why? Wars, like the one in America, have cost a fortune. The court of Versailles spends a lot on parties, buildings and gifts. Above all, the king has borrowed enormous sums: now he has to pay gigantic interest every year. Almost half of all spending goes to paying back debts!

In 1785, a scandal breaks out: the [Affair of the Diamond Necklace]. A swindler makes a cardinal believe that Marie Antoinette secretly wants to buy an extraordinary diamond necklace, with 647 diamonds! The cardinal buys it on credit, but the necklace is stolen and taken apart. The queen had nothing to do with it, but the people believe she spends money without counting. She is nicknamed "Madame Deficit".

The problem is that the Third Estate already pays lots of taxes, while the clergy and the nobility pay very little. The king's ministers, like Calonne, suggest making everyone pay, even the privileged.

In 1787, Calonne gathers an assembly of important nobles, the "Notables", to ask them to agree. But they refuse to lose their privileges!

The judges of the [parlements], who are also nobles, oppose the king too. They say that only the Estates-General, a great assembly representing the three estates, can agree to new taxes.

The king is stuck. He has no money and nobody wants to pay. In August 1788, he gives in: he announces he will call the Estates-General, which have not met since 1614!

title: Hail, hunger and the Day of the Tiles
text:
The year 1788 is a terrible year for French peasants.

On 13 July 1788, a gigantic hailstorm sweeps across northern France. Hailstones as big as eggs destroy the wheat fields just before the harvest, over hundreds of kilometres. The crops are lost.

Then comes the winter of 1788–1789, one of the coldest of the century. The Seine freezes over, and the mills are stuck in the ice and can no longer grind grain. It is so cold that people die in the streets.

Wheat becomes scarce, and the price of bread shoots up. Bread is the main food of the French: a worker eats about a kilo of bread a day! By spring 1789, a poor family must spend almost all its wages on bread. Many are hungry.

In towns and in the countryside, [riots] break out. Hungry people attack markets and convoys of wheat.

Anger against those in power grows too. On 7 June 1788, in Grenoble, the king wants to dismiss the judges of the parlement who oppose him. The townspeople revolt: they climb onto the roofs and throw tiles at the king's soldiers! This is the "Day of the Tiles".

Soon after, the leading citizens of the Dauphiné region meet at Vizille and demand a meeting of the Estates-General, with as many deputies for the Third Estate as for the other two estates put together.

Hunger, anger and hope: everything is ready for things to change. Everyone expects great things from the Estates-General...

title: "What is the Third Estate?"
text:
At the start of 1789, all of France is talking about the Estates-General that are about to meet. One question matters a lot: how will they vote?

Traditionally, each estate votes separately and has one vote. The clergy and the nobility, who share the same interests, would therefore always have two votes against one for the Third Estate, even though it represents almost all the people!

The Third Estate asks for two things: to have as many deputies as the other two estates put together (this is called "doubling"), and to vote "by head", meaning that each deputy has one vote.

The king agrees to the doubling: there will be about 600 deputies for the Third Estate, 300 for the clergy and 300 for the nobility. But he says nothing about how they will vote...

In January 1789, a priest, Abbé Sieyès, publishes a little booklet, a [pamphlet], which is a huge success. It is called What Is the Third Estate? and it begins like this:

"What is the Third Estate? Everything.
What has it been until now in the political order? Nothing.
What does it ask? To become something."

Sieyès explains that it is the Third Estate that works, produces, trades and keeps the country alive. For him, the Third Estate alone is the whole [nation], and the privileged are useless.

These simple, powerful sentences are read and repeated everywhere. More than 30,000 copies are sold in a few weeks. Thousands of other pamphlets are published.

Abbé Sieyès will be elected deputy for the Third Estate of Paris, and he will play a very important role in the Revolution... right up to the end, in 1799!

title: The books of grievances
text:
To prepare for the Estates-General, the king does something extraordinary: he asks the French people to say what is wrong!

In spring 1789, in every village, every town and every guild, people meet, often in the church. They elect their representatives and together write their complaints and wishes in notebooks. These are called the [cahiers de doléances], or "books of grievances". A grievance is a complaint.

There are about 60,000 of them! It is like a giant survey of France in 1789. You can still read them today in the archives.

What do the French ask for?

Peasants complain about taxes that are too heavy, about the tithe, about feudal dues, about the corvée (the unpaid work they must do for their lord), and about the lord's pigeons and rabbits that eat their crops, while they themselves are not allowed to hunt!

Many ask that everyone should pay taxes, including nobles and the clergy. Others ask for an end to lettres de cachet, for freedom of the press, for equal justice for all, or for the same weights and measures everywhere.

Almost nobody asks for an end to the monarchy. On the contrary, the cahiers are often very respectful towards the king, who is called "our good king". People think it is his ministers who are deceiving him.

But everyone hopes for great changes. For the first time, millions of French people have been asked for their opinion and have spoken out.

The deputies set off for Versailles with these books and lots of hope.

title: The Estates-General open
text:
On 5 May 1789, in Versailles, the [Estates-General] open in a large hall, the Hôtel des Menus-Plaisirs. About 1,200 deputies are there.

From the very start, the differences between the estates are obvious. The deputies of the clergy wear beautiful purple or black robes. The nobles wear silk clothes embroidered with gold, feathered hats and swords. The deputies of the Third Estate must wear a plain black suit and come in through a small side door!

King Louis XVI gives a speech. Then his finance minister, Necker, speaks for three hours... only about numbers and money! The Third Estate deputies are disappointed: they came to change France, not just to find money.

The real problem soon arrives: how should they vote? By estate (one vote per estate) or by head (one vote per deputy)? The clergy and nobility want to vote by estate. The Third Estate refuses.

For more than a month, nothing moves forward. The Third Estate deputies invite the others to join them and work together. A few parish priests, who are close to ordinary people, come and join them.

On 17 June 1789, the Third Estate deputies make a bold decision. They declare that they represent 96% of the nation and that from now on they are the [National Assembly]!

It is a revolutionary act: they are saying that power comes from the people, not from the king. They have not asked anyone's permission.

Some of these deputies will become famous: the great speaker Mirabeau, Abbé Sieyès, the astronomer Bailly... and an almost unknown young lawyer from Arras, Maximilien Robespierre.

title: The Tennis Court Oath
refs: Honoré Gabriel Riqueti, comte de Mirabeau
text:
On the morning of 20 June 1789, it is raining in Versailles. The deputies of the brand-new National Assembly arrive at their meeting hall... and find the door locked and guarded by soldiers! They are told the hall is closed for repairs.

The deputies think the king wants to stop them from meeting. They are furious. Where can they go?

Nearby is a large hall where people play [real tennis] (jeu de paume in French), the ancestor of tennis. The deputies head there. There are no chairs, just a few benches. The president of the Assembly, the astronomer Jean-Sylvain Bailly, climbs onto a table.

There, the deputies swear a solemn oath: they swear "never to separate" and to meet wherever necessary "until the [constitution] of the kingdom is established".

A constitution is a text that sets the rules of power: who makes the laws, and what rights citizens have. The king would no longer be able to do whatever he wants.

All the deputies raise their arms and take the oath. Only one refuses. The painter Jacques-Louis David showed this scene in a large, famous painting.

Three days later, on 23 June, the king orders the deputies to split up and meet by estate. The Third Estate stays seated. When one of the king's messengers reminds them of the order, Mirabeau replies, according to tradition:

"Go and tell those who sent you that we are here by the will of the people, and that we will leave only by the force of bayonets!"

The king finally gives in. On 27 June, he orders the clergy and nobility to join the Assembly. The people have won a first battle, without violence.

title: The storming of the Bastille
text:
In early July 1789, the king brings about 20,000 soldiers to the area around Paris and Versailles. On 11 July, he dismisses Necker, the popular minister. The people of Paris are afraid: does the king want to break up the Assembly by force?

On 12 July, in the garden of the Palais-Royal, a young journalist, Camille Desmoulins, climbs onto a table and shouts: "To arms, citizens!" The crowd is stirred up. Parisians look for weapons to defend themselves.

On the morning of 14 July, thousands of people go to the Invalides and take about 30,000 muskets and some cannons. But they need gunpowder! It is stored in the Bastille.

The Bastille is an old fortress with eight big towers, used as a prison. People were sometimes locked up there simply on the king's orders, with a lettre de cachet. For the people, it is the symbol of the king's [arbitrary] power.

The crowd surrounds the fortress and asks the governor, de Launay, for the gunpowder. He refuses. At about 1:30 pm, the defenders fire on the crowd. The fighting lasts several hours. About a hundred attackers are killed. Then some soldiers join the people, bringing cannons. At about 5 pm, the governor surrenders. The Bastille has fallen!

Inside, only seven prisoners are found. But the symbol is enormous: the people have defeated the king's power. Sadly, the governor and a few defenders are killed by the angry crowd.

That evening, according to a famous story, the king asked: "Is it a revolt?" And the Duke of La Rochefoucauld replied: "No, Sire, it is a revolution!"

The very next day, a builder named Palloy starts demolishing the fortress. He sells its stones as souvenirs all over France!

Since 1880, 14 July has been France's [national holiday]. In English, it is often called Bastille Day.

title: The Great Fear in the countryside
text:
After the fall of the Bastille, the news spreads all over France. But back then there were no telephones and no radio: news travelled on horseback or by word of mouth, and it got twisted along the way...

In the countryside, at the end of July 1789, a rumour runs from village to village: "brigands", paid by the nobles, are coming to destroy the crops to starve the people and punish the revolution!

These brigands do not exist. But the fear is very real. This is called the [Great Fear]. Peasants ring the tocsin (the alarm bells) and grab pitchforks, scythes and old muskets to defend themselves.

Since the brigands never come, the peasants' anger turns against the lords. In many regions, they attack castles. They do not always want to kill or loot: above all, they are looking for the "terriers", the old registers listing everything they owe the lords. They burn them on big bonfires!

Some castles are set on fire. Frightened nobles start leaving France: these are the first [émigrés].

In towns, the bourgeois create a [National Guard], a citizens' militia, to keep order and protect the revolution. In Paris, it is led by Lafayette.

This is also when the tricolour [cockade] appears: blue and red, the colours of the city of Paris, are combined with white, the colour of the king. These are the colours of the future French flag!

In Versailles, the deputies are worried about this violence in the countryside. They must do something to calm the peasants...

title: The night of 4 August: the end of privileges
text:
On the evening of 4 August 1789, in Versailles, the National Assembly meets. The deputies want to calm the rebellious peasants. They are about to live through an incredible night.

A young nobleman, the Viscount de Noailles, stands up and proposes that the nobles give up some of their rights over the peasants. Then the Duke d'Aiguillon, one of the richest lords in France, does the same.

Then a kind of excitement takes hold of the Assembly. One after another, deputies climb up to the speaker's platform to give up privileges!

The nobles give up the corvée, their special hunting rights, their dovecotes and their lords' courts. The clergy give up the tithe. Towns and provinces give up their special privileges. Everyone will be able to do any job, in the army as well as in the Church.

The session lasts until two in the morning. The deputies hug each other and weep with joy. They proclaim the king "restorer of French liberty".

In the following days, they write the decree that declares: "The National Assembly completely destroys the [feudal] system."

It is a revolution within the revolution! In one night, the society of three estates, which had existed for centuries, disappears. From now on, all French people are equal before the law and before taxes.

But careful, not everything is free: for some rights on land, the peasants will first have to pay the lords to buy them back. Many cannot afford it, and it is only in 1793 that these rights will be abolished without any payment.

But the night of 4 August remains in history as the end of privileges.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
refs: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

title: The women bring the king to Paris
text:
In autumn 1789, bread is still scarce in Paris and very expensive. Mothers queue for hours outside bakeries.

What's more, the king is hesitating to accept the Declaration of Rights and the decisions of 4 August. And people say that at a banquet in Versailles, officers trampled on the tricolour cockade! Parisians are furious.

On the morning of 5 October 1789, thousands of women, mostly market sellers from Les Halles and working women, gather outside the Paris City Hall. They decide to march to Versailles, 20 kilometres away, to ask the king for bread!

In the rain, about 6,000 to 7,000 women march towards Versailles, even dragging cannons. In the evening they are followed by Lafayette and 20,000 National Guards.

When they reach Versailles, the women burst into the Assembly. A delegation is received by the king, who promises to send wheat to Paris. He also agrees to sign the Declaration of Rights.

But early in the morning of 6 October, protesters get into the palace and reach the queen's rooms. Two guards are killed. Marie Antoinette escapes just in time through a secret passage to the king's bedroom!

Lafayette calms the crowd. The king appears on the balcony with his family. The crowd shouts: "To Paris! To Paris!"

The king has to agree. That same evening, a long procession brings the royal family back to Paris. The women sing: "We're bringing back the baker, the baker's wife and the baker's boy!" (the king, the queen and their son). The Assembly follows the king to Paris.

The king moves into the Tuileries Palace. From now on, he lives under the eyes of the Parisians. He is no longer really free.

title: France is divided into départements
text:
Before the Revolution, France was a real puzzle! It was divided into provinces of very different sizes, like Brittany, Provence or Normandy. Each one had its own laws, its own taxes, its own customs posts and even its own measurements. There were more than 700 different units of measurement in the kingdom!

The revolutionaries want a simpler, fairer and more equal country, where the same rules apply everywhere.

In 1790, the Assembly decides to divide France into 83 [départements] of roughly the same size. The idea is simple: from any village, you should be able to ride to the main town of the département in one day at most.

So as not to remind people of the old provinces, the départements are given names taken from nature: rivers (Seine, Loire, Gironde, Somme...), mountains (Jura, Vosges, Pyrenees...), or the sea (Finistère, which means "the end of the earth").

Each département is divided into districts and [communes]. Every village and every town becomes a commune, with an elected mayor. There are about 44,000 of them!

The départements still exist today! There are now 101 of them, including those overseas. Their number, which comes from alphabetical order, used to be on car number plates and is still in postcodes.

The revolutionaries also make the laws the same everywhere, remove the customs posts inside the country and prepare a single system of measurement for everyone: the future metric system.

It is one of the Revolution's reforms that has lasted best.

title: The Revolution and the Church
text:
The kingdom still has enormous debts. Where can money be found? The revolutionaries look towards the Catholic Church, which owns about 6% of the land in France: fields, forests, abbeys...

In November 1789, following a proposal by Talleyrand, a bishop, the Assembly decides that the Church's property now belongs to the nation. These are called the [national properties] (biens nationaux). They are sold at auction to pay off the debts. It is mostly bourgeois and well-off peasants who buy them.

In exchange, the state promises to pay the priests and to look after the poor and the sick, which the Church used to do.

Then, in July 1790, the Assembly votes for the [Civil Constitution of the Clergy]. It completely reorganises the Church in France: one bishop per département and, above all, parish priests and bishops will now be elected by citizens, like other public officials!

Priests must swear an oath of loyalty to the nation, to the law and to the king, and to this constitution.

This is the start of a great division. The Pope condemns the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. About half the priests agree to take the oath: they are called "jurors" or "constitutional priests". The other half refuse: these are the [refractory priests].

In many villages, the faithful are torn: should they go to the Mass of the priest who took the oath, or of the one who refused? Many Catholics who had supported the Revolution start to distrust it.

King Louis XVI, who is very religious, is troubled too. This religious question is one of the reasons that will later push some regions, like the Vendée, to rebel.

title: The Festival of the Federation
text:
One year after the fall of the Bastille, the revolutionaries want to celebrate the unity of all French people around the nation. A great festival is organised: the Festival of the Federation.

It takes place in Paris, on the Champ de Mars, where the Eiffel Tower stands today. This big field has to be turned into a huge amphitheatre, with banks of earth so that 300,000 people can sit down!

The work falls behind schedule. So thousands of Parisians come to help as volunteers: men, women, children, bourgeois, workers, monks, and even nobles and elegant ladies push wheelbarrows and use shovels, singing "Ah! ça ira, ça ira, ça ira!" ("It'll be fine!").

On 14 July 1790, despite the rain, about 300,000 spectators gather. Delegates of the National Guard, the "fédérés", have come from every département of France.

In the middle stands the "Altar of the Fatherland". Bishop Talleyrand celebrates Mass there. Then Lafayette, on a white horse, swears an oath in everyone's name: loyalty "to the nation, to the law and to the king".

Next, King Louis XVI swears in turn to respect the constitution. The queen lifts up her five-year-old son, the dauphin, in her arms. The crowd applauds and shouts: "Long live the king! Long live the nation!"

Similar festivals take place all over France. People dance, hug and share meals.

It is the happiest and most united moment of the Revolution. Many think the Revolution is over and that the king and the people are reconciled.

Today, France's national holiday on 14 July officially commemorates both the fall of the Bastille and this Festival of the Federation.

title: The king's flight to Varennes
text:
Louis XVI does not really accept the Revolution. He feels like a prisoner in the Tuileries, and he is troubled by the measures against the Church. In secret, he prepares to escape.

His plan: to leave Paris and reach Montmédy, near the border, where a loyal army is waiting. From there, he could negotiate from a position of strength, perhaps with the help of Austria, the queen's homeland.

On the night of 20 to 21 June 1791, the royal family secretly leaves the Tuileries in disguise. The king is dressed as a valet, the queen as a governess, and the children pretend to be the children of a Russian baroness. They climb into a large, heavily loaded and slow carriage called a "berline".

The journey falls behind schedule. At Sainte-Menehould, the postmaster, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, looks closely at one traveller. He compares him to the king's portrait printed on banknotes... It's him!

Drouet gallops along shortcuts and reaches Varennes before the carriage. He raises the alarm. On the evening of 21 June, the royal family is arrested in the little town of Varennes-en-Argonne.

The journey back to Paris takes four days. All along the way, a silent and hostile crowd watches the king go by. In Paris, posters say: "Anyone who applauds the king will be beaten; anyone who insults him will be hanged."

It is a huge shock. The king has broken the promise he made at the Festival of the Federation. Many French people no longer trust him.

For the first time, some dare to call for an end to the monarchy and for a [republic]. But the Assembly prefers to pretend that the king was "kidnapped", in order to keep the constitutional monarchy.

title: The Champ de Mars massacre
text:
After the flight to Varennes, Parisians argue passionately. In the political [clubs], like the Cordeliers Club or the Jacobin Club, people debate every evening.

At the Cordeliers Club, revolutionaries like Danton, Marat and Desmoulins think the king is a traitor and must be replaced. They write a [petition] asking for the king to be put on trial and for a new government to be organised.

On Sunday 17 July 1791, thousands of Parisians go to the Champ de Mars to sign this petition on the Altar of the Fatherland, where the Festival of the Federation had taken place a year earlier.

But the Assembly has decided to keep the king. The Mayor of Paris, Bailly, and the commander of the National Guard, Lafayette, see this gathering as dangerous. They declare "martial law" and have the red flag raised, which means force may be used.

The National Guard arrives at the Champ de Mars. Stones are thrown. The guards fire on the crowd. Dozens are killed, perhaps around fifty.

It is the first time revolutionaries have shot at other revolutionaries. Supporters of the constitutional monarchy and supporters of a republic are now enemies.

Many republican leaders hide or flee for a while. The Jacobin Club splits: the moderates leave it to found the Feuillants Club.

For Bailly and Lafayette, once heroes of the people, it is the end of their popularity. The people of Paris will never forgive them. Bailly will be guillotined in 1793, on the Champ de Mars, at the very spot of the massacre.

title: Olympe de Gouges and women's rights
refs: Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen
text:
Women played a big part in the Revolution: they demonstrated, marched on Versailles, founded clubs and wrote in newspapers. And yet the Declaration of the Rights of Man does not mention them, and they are not allowed to vote.

One woman decides to protest: Olympe de Gouges. Born in 1748 in Montauban, into a modest family, she is widowed very young and moves to Paris, where she becomes a writer. She writes plays, including one against the slavery of Black people, which is very brave at the time.

In September 1791, she publishes the [Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen]. She takes the 1789 Declaration article by article, but adds women. The first article says:

"Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights."

She also writes a sentence that has become famous: "Woman has the right to mount the scaffold; she must equally have the right to mount the speaker's platform." In other words: if a woman can be punished like a man, she must also be able to take part in politics like a man!

She asks for the right to vote, equality in marriage, the right to divorce, and recognition for children born outside marriage.

Other women fight too, like Théroigne de Méricourt or Pauline Léon, who demand the right to carry weapons.

The Revolution brings some progress: in 1792, marriage becomes a civil ceremony and divorce is allowed, on equal terms for husband and wife. Girls inherit as much as boys.

But women do not get the right to vote. In 1793, women's clubs are even banned.

Olympe de Gouges, who criticises Robespierre, is guillotined on 3 November 1793. French women will have to wait until 1944 to win the right to vote.

title: France's first Constitution
text:
Ever since the Tennis Court Oath in June 1789, the deputies had promised to give France a [constitution]. It took them more than two years of work!

On 3 September 1791, the first written Constitution in French history is finally finished. It begins with the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

France becomes a [constitutional monarchy]: there is still a king, but he no longer has all the power. He is no longer called "King of France" but "King of the French". His power now comes from the nation, and no longer from God.

Powers are separated, as Montesquieu wanted:
- the power to make laws belongs to a Legislative Assembly of 745 elected deputies;
- the king leads the government and chooses the ministers;
- judges, who are also elected, carry out justice.

The king has a "suspensive veto": he can block a law for a few years, but not forever.

But not everyone can vote! Only men over 25 who pay a certain amount of tax are "active citizens". The poorest, servants and all women are "passive citizens": they have rights, but they do not vote. This is called [property-based voting].

On 14 September 1791, Louis XVI swears loyalty to the Constitution in front of the Assembly. The Constituent Assembly breaks up. Its members had decided they could not be re-elected, so the new Legislative Assembly is made up of new men.

Many think the Revolution is complete. But the king has not really accepted this new system, and war is coming...

This constitution will last only one year.

title: France declares war on Austria
text:
The kings of Europe watch the French Revolution with worry. What if their own peoples wanted to rebel too? In August 1791, the Emperor of Austria, Marie Antoinette's brother, and the King of Prussia declare that they are ready to help Louis XVI.

Across the border, in Koblenz, thousands of noble [émigrés] form an army to come back to France and restore the Old Regime.

In the Legislative Assembly, a group of deputies, later called the [Girondins] (because several come from the Gironde region), wants war. Their leader, Brissot, thinks France should go and free the peoples of Europe from their kings, and unmask the traitors.

Strangely, the king and queen want war too, but for a different reason: they hope France will be beaten and that foreign armies will come to rescue them!

Only a few, like Robespierre, are against it. He says: "Nobody loves armed missionaries."

On 20 April 1792, France declares war on the "King of Bohemia and Hungary", in other words on Austria. Prussia joins Austria.

The start is a disaster. The French army is disorganised: many noble officers have emigrated. Some soldiers panic and run away. The enemies approach the border.

In July 1792, the Assembly proclaims: "The fatherland is in danger!" All citizens are called to sign up as volunteers. Tens of thousands of young men enlist.

This war will go on, almost without stopping, until 1815! It will make the Revolution harsher and more violent, because people start seeing traitors everywhere.

title: La Marseillaise
text:
On the night of 25 to 26 April 1792, a few days after war is declared, a young army engineer, Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle, is in Strasbourg. The mayor of the city has asked him to write a song to encourage the soldiers of the Army of the Rhine.

In one night, Rouget de Lisle writes the words and music of a war song. He calls it the "War Song for the Army of the Rhine".

The song begins like this:
"Allons enfants de la Patrie,
Le jour de gloire est arrivé!"
("Arise, children of the Fatherland, the day of glory has arrived!")

People love the song and it spreads fast. It reaches Marseille. In July 1792, volunteers from Marseille, the "[fédérés]", set off on foot for Paris, more than 800 kilometres away. They sing this song all along the way. When they arrive in Paris at the end of July, they sing it in the streets.

The Parisians love it and call it "the song of the Marseillais", and then simply "La Marseillaise".

It becomes the song of the Revolution. People sing it in battles, at festivals and in the streets. On 14 July 1795, it becomes the national song.

Under Napoleon and the kings who come back afterwards, it is banned because it is too revolutionary. It becomes France's [national anthem] again in 1879, and it still is today.

Its words are very warlike, because they were written during a war, when France was being invaded. Today some people think they are too violent; others point out that they are about defending liberty against tyrants.

La Marseillaise is known all over the world as a song of freedom.

title: The fall of the monarchy
text:
In summer 1792, the situation is explosive. Enemy armies are approaching. The king has used his veto to block several laws. Many Parisians think he is betraying France and is in contact with the enemy.

On 1 August, Paris learns about a declaration by the Duke of Brunswick, commander of the Prussian army: if anyone harms the royal family, Paris will be destroyed! Instead of frightening the Parisians, this threat makes them angry.

The [sans-culottes] get ready. They are called this ("without knee-breeches") because they wear long trousers instead of the short breeches and silk stockings of nobles and rich bourgeois. They are craftsmen, shopkeepers and workers. They often wear a red cap.

On the night of 9 to 10 August 1792, the alarm bells ring across Paris. A new revolutionary [Commune|paris commune] takes power at the City Hall.

On the morning of 10 August, thousands of sans-culottes and fédérés, including the men from Marseille, attack the Tuileries Palace, where the king lives. The palace is defended by Swiss Guards.

The king and his family leave the palace to take refuge in the Assembly. But fighting breaks out. It is very violent: hundreds of Swiss Guards and attackers are killed.

That same evening, the Assembly suspends the king. A few days later, the royal family is locked up in the Temple tower, an old fortress.

It is the end of the monarchy in France, after more than a thousand years of kings! The Assembly decides to elect a new assembly, the [National Convention], to write a new constitution. For the first time, all men will be able to vote, rich or poor: this is [universal suffrage] for men.

title: The September massacres
text:
The Revolution also had some very dark moments. We need to talk about them honestly.

At the end of August 1792, the news is terrible. The Prussians have crossed the border and taken the town of Longwy. On 2 September, people learn that they are besieging Verdun, the last fortress before Paris.

Parisians are afraid. Many men leave as volunteers to go and fight. A rumour spreads: while the soldiers are at the front, the prisoners in Paris jails, including refractory priests and nobles, will break out, massacre the volunteers' families and hand Paris over to the enemy!

The minister Danton calls for energy: "Boldness, more boldness, always boldness, and France will be saved!"

From 2 to 6 September 1792, armed gangs burst into the prisons of Paris. They set up quick, fake courts, then kill the prisoners. Between 1,100 and 1,400 people are massacred, many of them priests, but also ordinary criminals, women and even children.

Among the victims is the Princess de Lamballe, a friend of Marie Antoinette.

The authorities do almost nothing to stop the massacres. Some journalists, like Marat, even encouraged them.

These massacres horrify part of France and Europe. They show how fear and rumours can push ordinary people to commit terrible crimes.

Historians still study today how such violence was possible. Remembering these moments helps us understand why justice must always be carried out by real judges, according to the law.

title: The victory at Valmy
text:
In September 1792, the Prussian army advances towards Paris. It is considered the best army in Europe, with very well-trained soldiers. Facing it, the French army is made up of the king's former soldiers and lots of young, inexperienced volunteers.

On 20 September 1792, the two armies face each other near the village of Valmy, in Champagne. The French army, commanded by Generals Kellermann and Dumouriez, is on a hill, next to a windmill.

It has been raining for several days. The ground is muddy. The battle begins with a long cannonade: both sides fire at each other with their cannons. The excellent French artillery holds firm.

The Prussians advance to attack. Then General Kellermann puts his hat on the tip of his sabre, raises it to the sky and shouts: "Long live the nation!" The whole army takes up his cry. The soldiers do not step back.

Surprised by this courage, the Prussians stop, then pull back. The rain and illness (many Prussian soldiers have dysentery) discourage them too. A few days later, they head back home.

It is not a big battle: few people died, about 300 on the French side. But it is a huge victory! For the first time, an army of citizens, fighting for the nation and for liberty, has stopped an army of kings.

The great German writer Goethe, who was with the Prussian army, is said to have declared that evening: "From this place and from this day begins a new era in the history of the world."

Paris is saved. And the next day, something very important happens...

title: The birth of the Republic
text:
On 20 September 1792, the very day of the victory at Valmy, a new assembly meets for the first time in Paris: the National Convention. Its 749 deputies were elected by all men, rich or poor.

The next day, 21 September 1792, the Convention takes its first decision, unanimously: "Royalty is abolished in France."

On 22 September, it decides to date official documents "Year I of the Republic". France has become a [republic]! This is the First Republic.

In a republic, there is no king. Power belongs to the people, who elect their representatives. King Louis XVI is now just an ordinary citizen: he is now called "Louis Capet", after his distant ancestor Hugh Capet.

The Republic adopts new symbols:
- the blue, white and red flag;
- the motto "Liberty, Equality", to which "Fraternity" will be added later;
- a woman wearing a red Phrygian cap, the symbol of liberty, who will later be called Marianne;
- the Gallic rooster, already an old symbol of France.

People no longer say "Monsieur" or "Madame", but "Citizen". Many use the informal "tu" with each other to show they are equal.

In the Convention, two big groups soon clash: the Girondins, who are more moderate and rely on the départements, and the [Montagnards], who are more radical, sit at the top of the assembly on the highest benches (the "Mountain"), and rely on the sans-culottes of Paris. Among them are Robespierre, Danton and Marat.

The question that divides everyone: what should be done with the king?

title: The trial and execution of Louis XVI
text:
In November 1792, an "iron chest", a secret hiding place containing the king's letters, is discovered in the Tuileries. The letters prove that he was in contact with the enemies of the Revolution. The Convention decides to put Louis XVI on trial.

The trial begins in December 1792. The Convention itself acts as the court. The king, called "Louis Capet", is accused of "conspiracy against the liberty of the nation".

He is defended by three lawyers, including old Malesherbes, aged 71, who bravely offered to defend him. Louis XVI calmly answers the questions.

The deputies vote one by one, out loud, in front of everyone. Almost all of them find him guilty. Then comes the question of the sentence. The vote lasts more than 24 hours. Death is voted by a narrow majority: 387 votes to 334.

On the morning of 21 January 1793, Louis XVI is driven in a carriage across Paris to the Place de la Révolution (today the Place de la Concorde). Thousands of soldiers line the streets. He is calm and brave.

On the scaffold, he tries to speak to the crowd: "I die innocent of all the crimes I am accused of. I forgive those who are causing my death." But the drums drown out his voice.

He is executed with the [guillotine], a machine presented as faster and less cruel than the old methods of execution, and the same for everyone.

The king's execution shocks all of Europe. Foreign kings, especially in England and Spain, go to war against France. In France too, many people are deeply upset.

Today, France has abolished the death penalty, since 1981.

title: The war in the Vendée
text:
In February 1793, the Republic, at war with almost all of Europe, needs lots of soldiers. The Convention decides to raise 300,000 men. In every commune, young unmarried men must be chosen by lottery to join the army.

In western France, in the region called the Vendée, the peasants refuse. They do not want to go and fight far from home. They are also very Catholic and loyal to their refractory priests, who are being persecuted by the Revolution. And they are disappointed: the Revolution has not brought them much.

In March 1793, thousands of peasants rebel. They take up arms and choose as leaders local nobles, like La Rochejaquelein, or ordinary people, like Cathelineau, a travelling pedlar. Their army is called the "Catholic and Royal Army". On their chests they wear a red heart topped with a cross, the Sacred Heart.

At first, the Vendéans win many victories against the republican armies. But in December 1793, they are crushed.

Then the repression is terrible. In 1794, the Convention sends the [infernal columns]: troops that march through the region burning villages and killing the inhabitants, including women and children. In Nantes, thousands of prisoners are drowned in the Loire.

The war in the Vendée killed about 170,000 people on the Vendéan side, and tens of thousands on the republican side. It is a true [civil war], where French people fight other French people.

In Brittany and Normandy, other rebels, the "Chouans", fight a guerrilla war against the Republic.

Peace only really returns in 1800. The memory of these events is still very much alive in western France.

title: The Committee of Public Safety
text:
In spring 1793, the Republic is in danger on every side. Almost all of Europe is at war with it: Austria, Prussia, England, Spain, Holland... The Vendée has rebelled. Bread is expensive, and the sans-culottes of Paris are angry.

To govern faster and more firmly, in April 1793 the Convention creates a small group of deputies to run the country: the [Committee of Public Safety]. "Public safety" means "saving the country".

The Committee has twelve members. They meet every day, often late into the night, in the Tuileries Palace. They run the war, the police, the economy and relations with other countries.

In June 1793, armed sans-culottes surround the Convention and force the deputies to arrest the Girondin leaders. The [Montagnards] take power. Several regions, like Lyon, Marseille or Bordeaux, rebel against Paris.

In July 1793, Maximilien Robespierre joins the Committee. He is a lawyer from Arras, very hard-working and always elegant, nicknamed "the Incorruptible" because nobody can ever bribe him. He defends the poor and democracy, but he also becomes more and more merciless towards those he sees as enemies of the Revolution.

Other members include Saint-Just, a young man of 25, Couthon, and Carnot, an engineer who organises the armies. Carnot manages to raise more than a million soldiers with the "levée en masse" (mass call-up) of August 1793.

The Committee gets results: enemy armies are pushed back and the revolts are crushed. But to achieve this, it sets up an emergency government, without elections, which will use fear as a weapon.

title: The death of Marat
text:
Jean-Paul Marat is one of the most famous and most feared revolutionaries. A doctor and scientist, he has become a journalist. His newspaper, The Friend of the People, fiercely denounces everyone he sees as a traitor and often calls for them to be killed. The sans-culottes adore him. His enemies hate him.

Marat suffers from a very painful skin disease. To soothe it, he spends long hours in a bathtub filled with water and medicine, where he keeps on writing on a board laid across the tub.

Charlotte Corday is a 24-year-old woman from Caen, in Normandy. She supports the Girondins, who have been driven out of the Convention. To her, Marat is to blame for the violence and the civil war. She thinks that by killing him, she will bring back peace.

She comes to Paris and buys a knife. On 13 July 1793, she turns up at Marat's home saying she has information about traitors. Marat receives her in his bathtub. While he is writing down names, she stabs him. He dies almost at once.

Charlotte Corday does not try to escape. At her trial, she declares: "I killed one man to save a hundred thousand." She is guillotined four days later.

But she was wrong: Marat's death does not bring peace. On the contrary, he becomes a [martyr] of the Revolution, and his supporters demand even more severity.

The painter Jacques-Louis David, Marat's friend, paints a famous picture: The Death of Marat. It shows Marat dead in his bathtub, his pen still in his hand. It is one of the best-known paintings of the Revolution. Today it hangs in Brussels.

title: The Louvre becomes a museum for everyone
text:
For centuries, the finest paintings and statues in France belonged to the king. They decorated his palaces, and only nobles and guests could admire them.

The revolutionaries think these treasures should belong to the nation, that is, to everyone. They also want works of art to help educate the people.

On 10 August 1793, for the first anniversary of the fall of the monarchy, the "Central Museum of the Arts" opens its doors in the Louvre Palace, the old palace of the kings in Paris. This is the birth of the Louvre [museum]!

Entry is free. The museum is open to all: rich and poor, French people and foreigners. Some days are kept for artists who come to copy the works to learn how to paint.

At first, about 500 paintings are shown, masterpieces from the royal collections, like those of Leonardo da Vinci or Raphael. The Mona Lisa, though, only arrives there in 1797.

The Revolution also creates other great institutions for knowledge:
- the National Museum of Natural History, in 1793, with its zoo in the Jardin des Plantes;
- the National Conservatory of Arts and Crafts, for inventions and machines;
- the École Polytechnique, to train engineers;
- the National Archives and the National Library, open to the public.

But the Revolution also destroyed many works of art. Statues of kings were pulled down and churches looted. At Notre-Dame de Paris, the statues of the kings of Judah were beheaded, because people thought they were kings of France! A priest, Abbé Grégoire, then invented the word "[vandalism]" to denounce this destruction.

Today, the Louvre is the most visited museum in the world.

title: The Terror
text:
On 5 September 1793, sans-culottes burst into the Convention. They demand bread and harsh measures against the enemies of the Revolution. One deputy cries: "Let us make Terror the order of the day!"

This is the start of the darkest period of the Revolution: the [Terror]. The leaders' idea is that the enemies of the Republic must be frightened in order to save it.

On 17 September 1793, the Convention votes for the [Law of Suspects]. It allows the arrest of anyone "suspected" of being against the Revolution: nobles, their families, relatives of émigrés, former officials, but also anyone who has criticised the government or not shown enough enthusiasm. Sometimes all it takes is a neighbour reporting you!

More than 300,000 people are arrested. The prisons are full.

Suspects are tried by the [Revolutionary Tribunal], in Paris and in other cities. Trials are very quick, and the accused have few ways to defend themselves. Many are sentenced to death and guillotined.

About 17,000 people are executed after a trial, and many others die in prison or are killed without a trial, especially in the rebel regions. In total, it is estimated that the Terror claimed several tens of thousands of victims. Some were nobles, but most were ordinary people: peasants, craftsmen...

Revolutionaries themselves become victims: the Girondins, and then Danton and his friends, who were asking for the Terror to stop, are guillotined in April 1794.

At the same time, the government sets a maximum price for bread and basic goods, to help the poor.

The Terror remains an example of what happens when, in the name of a good cause, people's freedoms and their right to defend themselves are taken away.

title: The Republican calendar
text:
The revolutionaries want to change everything, even time! For them, the usual calendar is too closely tied to religion and kings: the days carry saints' names, and the years are counted from the birth of Jesus.

In October 1793, the Convention adopts a new calendar: the [Republican calendar]. Year I begins on 22 September 1792, the day the Republic was born.

The year is divided into 12 months of 30 days. The poet Fabre d'Églantine gives them poetic names linked to nature and the seasons:
- in autumn: Vendémiaire (grape harvest), Brumaire (mist), Frimaire (frost);
- in winter: Nivôse (snow), Pluviôse (rain), Ventôse (wind);
- in spring: Germinal (sprouting seeds), Floréal (flowers), Prairial (meadows);
- in summer: Messidor (harvest), Thermidor (heat), Fructidor (fruit).

Since 12 × 30 = 360, there are 5 or 6 days left at the end of the year: these are the "Sansculottides", festival days.

No more 7-day weeks! Each month is divided into three "[décades]" of 10 days: primidi, duodi, tridi... up to décadi, the day of rest. That makes just one day off every 10 days instead of every 7, which workers do not like much!

Each day also has the name of a plant, an animal or a tool: carrot day, horse day, plough day...

They even tried to invent decimal hours: 10 hours a day and 100 minutes an hour! But that did not work.

The Republican calendar is used for 12 years. Napoleon abolishes it on 1 January 1806. But people still talk about it today: "9 Thermidor", "18 Brumaire"...

title: The fate of Marie Antoinette and her children
text:
After the execution of Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette remains a prisoner in the Temple tower with her children and her sister-in-law, Madame Élisabeth. She is now called "the Widow Capet".

Marie Antoinette is very unpopular. For years, pamphlets have blamed her for everything: for ruining France with her spending, for betraying the country to help Austria. People even put words in her mouth that she never said: "If they have no bread, let them eat cake!"

In July 1793, her son, Louis-Charles, aged 8, is taken away from her. For royalists, he is the new king, "Louis XVII". He is handed over to a shoemaker and kept locked up alone. He will be very badly treated and will die of illness in prison in 1795, aged 10.

In August, Marie Antoinette is moved to the Conciergerie, a prison on the Île de la Cité. In October 1793, she is tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal. She is accused of plotting with the enemy. Lying and hateful accusations are even made against her. She defends herself with dignity.

She is sentenced to death. On 16 October 1793, her hair is cut off, and she is taken in a plain cart to the Place de la Révolution. The painter David sketches her on the way. She is 37 years old.

On the scaffold, she accidentally steps on the executioner's foot and says to him: "Sir, I beg your pardon, I did not do it on purpose." These are said to be her last words.

Her daughter, Marie-Thérèse, nicknamed "Madame Royale", is the only survivor of the family. In 1795, she is exchanged for French prisoners and leaves for Austria.

Today, historians show that many of the accusations against Marie Antoinette were exaggerated or false.

title: The first abolition of slavery
text:
In 1789, France has colonies in the Caribbean, like Saint-Domingue (today Haiti), Guadeloupe and Martinique. Hundreds of thousands of Africans and their descendants are held there in [slavery]. They grow sugar cane and coffee in terrible conditions. Saint-Domingue is the richest colony in the world.

Yet the Declaration of the Rights of Man says that "men are born free and equal in rights"! Some revolutionaries, like Abbé Grégoire and the members of the "Society of the Friends of the Blacks", denounce this contradiction. But rich colonists and merchants from port cities like Bordeaux and Nantes are against abolition.

In August 1791, in Saint-Domingue, the enslaved people rise up in huge numbers. It is the biggest slave revolt in history. Among their leaders is a formerly enslaved man who had been freed, very intelligent and skilful: Toussaint Louverture.

In 1793, the Republic's commissioners in Saint-Domingue, like Sonthonax, proclaim freedom for the enslaved people of the island.

On 4 February 1794 (16 Pluviôse Year II), three deputies from Saint-Domingue, including a formerly enslaved man, Jean-Baptiste Belley, arrive at the Convention. That day, the Convention votes for the [abolition] of slavery in all French colonies! The formerly enslaved people become French citizens.

It is a historic decision, the first abolition of slavery by a major European country.

Sadly, Napoleon Bonaparte brings back slavery in 1802. But in Saint-Domingue, the formerly enslaved people fight back. Toussaint Louverture is captured and dies in prison in France, but his companions win the war: in 1804, Haiti becomes the first independent country founded by formerly enslaved people.

Slavery will only be abolished for good in France in 1848.

title: The Festival of the Supreme Being
refs: Dechristianization of France during the French Revolution
text:
In 1793, some revolutionaries want to get rid of the Christian religion: this is called [dechristianisation]. Churches are closed or turned into "temples of Reason". Priests are forced to give up their work. Church bells are melted down to make cannons. At Notre-Dame de Paris, a "Festival of Reason" is held, with an actress playing Liberty.

Robespierre does not like these excesses. He thinks the people need to believe in something, and that those who mock all religion are dangerous for morality. He is not Catholic, but he believes in a creator God, whom he calls the "Supreme Being", and in the immortality of the soul.

In May 1794, he has a decree voted: "The French people recognise the existence of the Supreme Being and the immortality of the soul."

On 8 June 1794 (20 Prairial Year II), a huge festival is held in Paris, designed by the painter David. Hundreds of thousands of Parisians take part. Women carry flowers, men carry oak branches.

Robespierre, president of the Convention, walks at the front in a blue coat, holding a bunch of flowers and ears of wheat. He sets fire to a big statue representing Atheism, and from under it appears a statue of Wisdom (a little blackened by the smoke!). Then the procession goes to the Champ de Mars, where an artificial mountain has been built with a Tree of Liberty on top.

But many deputies feel that Robespierre sees himself as a high priest or a dictator. Some make fun of him behind his back.

Two days later, a new law makes the Terror even more terrible. The deputies start to fear for their own lives...

title: 9 Thermidor: the fall of Robespierre
text:
In June and July 1794, the Terror is at its height. A law of 10 June has removed almost all the rights of the accused: no more lawyers, no more required witnesses. In Paris, more than 1,300 people are guillotined in just seven weeks. This is called the "Great Terror".

And yet the situation has improved: the French armies are winning. On 26 June 1794, they win a great victory at Fleurus, in Belgium. Many think the Terror is no longer needed.

On 26 July 1794 (8 Thermidor Year II), Robespierre gives a long speech to the Convention. He says there are still traitors among the deputies, but he refuses to name them. Every deputy wonders: "What if it's me?"

The next day, 27 July (9 Thermidor), the threatened deputies unite against him. When Robespierre tries to speak, they drown him out, shouting: "Down with the tyrant!" He is arrested along with his brother, Saint-Just and Couthon.

During the night, the Paris Commune, which supports Robespierre, frees them and takes them to the City Hall. But few sans-culottes come to defend them. Soldiers of the Convention take the City Hall. Robespierre is wounded in the jaw by a pistol shot.

On 28 July 1794 (10 Thermidor), Robespierre and 21 of his supporters are guillotined on the Place de la Révolution, without a trial. The next day, 71 more follow.

This is the end of the Terror. The prisons open, and thousands of suspects are released. The Revolutionary Tribunal is reformed, then abolished. The Jacobin Club is closed.

Historians still debate Robespierre today: a defender of the people and of democracy for some, a bloodthirsty tyrant for others.

title: Incroyables, Merveilleuses and a winter of famine
text:
After the fall of Robespierre, France breathes again. This period is called the "Thermidorian Reaction". The French want to forget their fear and have fun.

In Paris, rich young men, often sons of bourgeois families, get themselves noticed. They are called the "[Incroyables]" ("Incredibles") and the "Muscadins", because they wear musk perfume. They wear exaggerated clothes: huge cravats that come up to their noses, long hair on the sides, glasses, and a heavy lead-weighted stick they call their "executive power". They attack former Jacobins in the streets!

They also talk in a strange way: they do not pronounce the letter "r", which reminds them of the word "Revolution". They say "Ma pa'ole d'honneu'!" ("My wo'd of honou'!") or "C'est inc'oyable!" ("It's inc'edible!"). That is where their nickname comes from.

Fashionable young women, the "Merveilleuses" ("Marvellous Ones"), wear light, see-through dresses inspired by ancient Greece, and blond wigs. Balls are held everywhere. There are even "victims' balls", only for people who had a relative guillotined!

But while some are having fun, ordinary people are suffering. In December 1794, the maximum price of bread is scrapped. Prices soar. The paper money, the [assignat], is worth almost nothing. The winter of 1794–1795 is terribly cold. Many poor people die of hunger.

In spring 1795, starving sans-culottes burst into the Convention shouting: "Bread and the Constitution of 1793!" They are pushed back by the army. It is the end of the sans-culotte movement.

The Convention prepares a new constitution, which will give power to the richest and prevent any single man from becoming too powerful.

title: The metre: a measure for everyone
Young General Bonaparte takes the stage
text:
In 1795, the Convention finishes a new constitution. To stop the royalists from coming back, it decides that two thirds of the future deputies must be chosen from among the members of the Convention.

The [royalists], who wanted to take power through elections, are furious. They decide to rebel. On 5 October 1795 (13 Vendémiaire Year IV), about 25,000 armed rebels march on the Convention at the Tuileries.

To defend the assembly, the deputy Barras calls on a young general of 26, out of work at the time, whom he had met at the siege of Toulon: Napoleon Bonaparte.

Bonaparte was born in Corsica in 1769, into a family of minor nobility. He is an artillery officer, which means a cannon specialist. In 1793, he got noticed by helping to take the port of Toulon back from the British.

Bonaparte acts fast. He sends a cavalry officer, Murat, to fetch 40 cannons from a camp near Paris. He places them around the Tuileries.

When the rebels attack, especially in front of the church of Saint-Roch, on the Rue Saint-Honoré, Bonaparte has the cannons fire. In a few hours, the revolt is crushed. About 300 people are killed.

The royalists scornfully nickname him "General Vendémiaire". But for the Republic, he is a saviour. He becomes commander-in-chief of the Army of the Interior.

A few months later, in March 1796, he marries Joséphine de Beauharnais, an elegant widow whose first husband had been guillotined.

Nobody yet suspects that this little Corsican general will soon dominate France and all of Europe...

title: The Directory: five men in power
text:
After the Terror, the deputies are afraid that one man or a small group might become too powerful. So the new Constitution of Year III, adopted in 1795, shares power among many people.

The power to make laws is given to two assemblies:
- the Council of Five Hundred, which proposes laws;
- the Council of Ancients, 250 deputies over the age of 40, who accept or reject them.

The power to govern is given to five men, the "Directors". This government is called the [Directory]. Each year, one of the five is replaced. The most famous Director is Barras.

The right to vote is once again limited to men who pay taxes. And to be one of the electors who choose the deputies, you have to be quite rich. It is the bourgeoisie that governs.

The Directory lasts four years, but it is fragile. It is attacked from two sides: by royalists, who want a king back, and by former Jacobins, who want more equality.

In 1796, a revolutionary called Gracchus Babeuf prepares a plot, the "Conspiracy of the Equals", to share wealth among everyone. He is arrested and executed.

When the elections are won by royalists in 1797, the Directory calls on the army to cancel the results. It does it again in 1798 against the Jacobins. The government relies more and more on generals to stay in power.

The economy is doing badly, the roads are dangerous, and many leaders are accused of corruption.

Meanwhile, the French armies win great victories abroad, and the generals become more and more popular and powerful. One of them in particular...

title: Bonaparte's Italian campaign
text:
In 1796, France is still at war with Austria. The Directory gives Napoleon Bonaparte, only 26 years old, command of the Army of Italy. It is a small, poor, badly equipped army: the soldiers are short of shoes, clothes and food.

Bonaparte tells them: "Soldiers, you are naked and badly fed... I want to lead you into the most fertile plains in the world."

In a few weeks, he wins victory after victory against the Piedmontese and the Austrians in northern Italy. He moves very fast and always takes his enemies by surprise.

In November 1796, at Arcole, his soldiers hesitate to cross a bridge under Austrian fire. Bonaparte grabs a flag and charges onto the bridge himself! The painter Gros made this scene famous, even though in reality Bonaparte fell into a marsh during the battle.

In 1797, Austria signs the peace of [Campo Formio]. France gets Belgium and controls northern Italy, where Bonaparte creates "sister republics".

But this campaign also has a dark side: the French armies plunder Italy. Hundreds of works of art are sent to Paris, to the Louvre, and gold fills the Directory's treasury.

Bonaparte also understands how important his own image is. He has newspapers published that tell of his great deeds and present him as a hero. This is a form of [propaganda].

When he returns to Paris in December 1797, he is cheered as a hero. He has become the most popular man in France. The Directory starts to worry about this ambitious general...

title: The Egyptian expedition and the Rosetta Stone
refs: French campaign in Egypt and Syria
text:
In 1798, the Directory, rather pleased to send Bonaparte far away, gives him an extraordinary mission: to conquer Egypt! The aim is to cut off the British route to India, their richest colony.

In May 1798, a fleet of more than 300 ships leaves Toulon with 35,000 soldiers. But on board there are also about 160 scientists, engineers, draughtsmen and artists, whose job is to study Egypt: its plants, animals, monuments and history.

In July 1798, near the pyramids, Bonaparte defeats the Mamluks, horsemen who rule Egypt. He is said to have told his soldiers: "From the top of these pyramids, forty centuries are looking down on you!"

But a few days later, the British admiral Nelson destroys the French fleet at Aboukir. The French army is stuck in Egypt. The campaign becomes hard: heat, diseases like the plague, revolts...

The expedition's greatest success is scientific. In 1799, French soldiers building a fort near the town of Rosetta discover a large, dark engraved stone: the [Rosetta Stone]. It carries the same text written in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, demotic (another Egyptian script) and ancient Greek.

Thanks to this stone, a young French scholar, Jean-François Champollion, manages in 1822 to decipher [hieroglyphs], which nobody had been able to read for centuries! This is the birth of [Egyptology].

The scholars later publish the Description of Egypt, a huge illustrated encyclopedia.

In August 1799, Bonaparte learns that things are going badly in France. He leaves his army in Egypt and quietly returns to France. He has a plan...

title: The coup of 18 Brumaire
text:
In October 1799, Bonaparte returns from Egypt. Wherever he goes, crowds cheer him as a saviour. The Directory is very unpopular, and many people want a stronger government.

Abbé Sieyès, the author of What Is the Third Estate?, has become one of the five Directors. He wants to change the constitution and is looking for a general to help him. He chooses Bonaparte.

On 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire Year VIII), the plotters make the two assemblies believe that a Jacobin plot is threatening Paris. They persuade them to meet the next day at Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, protected by soldiers under Bonaparte's command. Three Directors resign.

The next day, 10 November (19 Brumaire), at Saint-Cloud, things go badly. Bonaparte gives a muddled speech to the Council of Ancients. Then he enters the Council of Five Hundred. The deputies shout: "Down with the dictator! Outlaw him!" Bonaparte is jostled and has to leave.

It is his brother Lucien, president of the Council of Five Hundred, who saves the day. He tells the soldiers that deputies armed with daggers have threatened their general. The grenadiers march into the hall with bayonets forward. The deputies flee, some through the windows!

In the evening, a few deputies who stayed behind vote to end the Directory. Power is handed to three [consuls]: Bonaparte, Sieyès and Roger Ducos. It is a [coup d'état].

A few days later, the consuls declare: "Citizens, the Revolution is fixed on the principles that began it. It is over."

Very soon, Bonaparte becomes First Consul and takes all the power. The Revolution is over. A new era begins.

title: The Civil Code keeps ideas from the Revolution
text:
Once he is First Consul, Bonaparte rules alone. In 1804, he has himself crowned Emperor of the French under the name Napoleon I. This is the end of the Republic. There is no longer real freedom of the press or free elections.

And yet Napoleon keeps an important part of the Revolution's legacy. He even says himself: "I am the Revolution."

His greatest achievement is the Civil Code, published on 21 March 1804. During the Revolution, the laws had changed a lot and were scattered. Napoleon asks legal experts to gather all the rules of everyday life into a single book, with 2,281 articles.

The Civil Code keeps several great principles of 1789:
- everyone is equal before the law: no more privileges of birth;
- freedom of conscience: you can follow the religion of your choice;
- the right to property: those who bought national properties keep them;
- civil marriage, celebrated at the town hall, and divorce.

But the Civil Code is not fair to women. A married woman must obey her husband and cannot do anything without his permission. This will not change until the 20th century.

Napoleon also creates other institutions that still exist: the [lycées] (high schools), prefects in each département, the Bank of France, and the Legion of Honour, a medal to reward merit.

The Civil Code is still largely the basis of French law today. Thanks to Napoleon's conquests, it was adopted or copied in many countries: Belgium, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Quebec, Louisiana, Latin America... and even Japan was inspired by it!

title: 14 July becomes the national holiday
text:
After the Revolution, France went through many different kinds of government: Napoleon's Empire, the return of the kings, a Second Republic, a Second Empire... For a long time, memories of the Revolution divided the French. Some admired it, others hated it.

In 1870, a Third Republic is proclaimed. The republicans want to give France shared symbols taken from the Revolution.

In 1879, La Marseillaise becomes the national anthem again. In 1880, the deputies have to choose a date for the national holiday. Which one?

They choose 14 July. The law of 6 July 1880 simply says: "The Republic adopts 14 July as the day of the annual national holiday."

But which 14 July? The one in 1789, the storming of the Bastille, a symbol of liberty won? Or the one in 1790, the Festival of the Federation, a symbol of the unity of the French? The deputies left the question open, so that everyone could see in it what they preferred. The storming of the Bastille also brought violence to mind, so moderates liked the Festival of the Federation better.

On 14 July 1880, the first national holiday is a great success. There are parades, dances, lights and banquets all over France.

Today, every 14 July, there is:
- a big [military parade] on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, in front of the President of the Republic, with planes drawing the tricolour flag in the sky;
- public dances, often at fire stations;
- and in the evening, fireworks in every town, including a magnificent display at the foot of the Eiffel Tower.

In English, this holiday is called "Bastille Day".

title: The symbols of the Republic
text:
Many of the symbols of France today were born during the Revolution. You see them every day without even thinking about it!

The tricolour flag: blue, white and red. It comes from the cockade of 1789, which combined the blue and red of Paris with the white of the king. It becomes the national flag in 1794, with the colours in this order, designed by the painter David.

The motto "[Liberty, Equality, Fraternity]". It was heard as early as the Revolution, but it only became the Republic's official motto in 1848, and then again under the Third Republic. It is written on town halls, schools, coins...

Marianne. She is a woman who represents the Republic. She often wears a red [Phrygian cap], a cap that in ancient times was worn by freed slaves: so it is a symbol of liberty. Her bust is in every town hall. Famous women have lent her their faces, like the actresses Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve. You can also see her on stamps.

La Marseillaise, the national anthem, written in 1792.

14 July, the national holiday.

The Gallic rooster, a very old symbol, was already used during the Revolution. Today you can see it on the shirts of French national sports teams.

But the legacy of the Revolution is also made of ideas: the sovereignty of the people (it is the people who choose their leaders), equality before the law, human rights, and [secularism], which was prepared by separating the state from religion.

Article 2 of today's French Constitution says: "The principle of the Republic is: government of the people, by the people and for the people."

title: The French Revolution in today's world
text:
The French Revolution did not just change France. It changed the world.

Its ideas crossed borders. In the 19th century, many peoples in Europe and Latin America rose up in the name of liberty and equality. La Marseillaise was sung by revolutionaries in many countries.

On 10 December 1948, in Paris, at the Palais de Chaillot, the United Nations adopts the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights]. Its first article echoes the one from 1789: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." A Frenchman, René Cassin, played a big part in writing it. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for this.

In 1989, France celebrates the [bicentenary] of the Revolution, that is, its 200th anniversary. On 14 July 1989, a huge parade-show crosses Paris, and an American singer, Jessye Norman, sings La Marseillaise wrapped in a tricolour flag on the Place de la Concorde.

That same year, in China and in Eastern Europe, crowds demand freedom. In November 1989, the Berlin Wall falls.

Historians keep on discussing the Revolution. It brought wonderful ideas: liberty, equality, human rights, the sovereignty of the people. But it also saw violence, civil war and the Terror.

It teaches us that freedom is precious and fragile, that rights must apply to everyone, including people we disagree with, and that change comes about better through debate and law than through violence.

Today, it is up to citizens, and so one day up to you, to keep these ideas alive: by voting, by debating, by respecting others. And you, what do you think of the Revolution?
